name: Eraulgo artea (the Encina de Eraul)
species: Holm Oak (Quercus ilex, register text specifies the ilex x ballota intergrade)

location.address: Beside the track from Eraul to Abartzuza, opposite the bend by the San Pedro hermitage, Eraul, Deierri/Valle de Yerri, Navarre
location.neighbourhood: Eraul (a hamlet of the Deierri/Valle de Yerri valley), about 500m east of the village on the track towards Abartzuza

access: Free, on open rural ground beside a public track between Eraul and Abartzuza; visible from the village street. No gate or ticket found in any source.
transport: Rural Navarre; no public transport reaches Eraul directly. Nearest town with services is Estella-Lizarra, about 8km south; a car is the realistic way to reach it.
verify_notes:
TWO SOURCES: (1) eu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eraulgo_artea, a full article giving species, dimensions, history and the 1991 designation; (2) Decreto Foral 87/2009 (Gobierno de Navarra), the CURRENT official register text at lexnavarra.navarra.es, which superseded the original 1991 decree and re-lists this tree as Monumento Natural 'M.N. 1, Encina de Eraul', species 'Quercus ilex L. subsp. ilex L. x Quercus ilex subsp. ballota (Desf.) Samp.', with UTM coords X=578421 Y=4729960 (zone 30N ETRS89). I hand-checked those UTM coordinates against Wikidata's lat/lon (42.71626, -2.04426, from the Wikipedia geohack link) by converting the easting: they land within roughly 100m of each other on longitude, so the two sources independently agree on a TREE-LEVEL point, not just 'the village of Eraul'. location_precision is 'confirmed' on that basis.

SPECIES: Wikipedia calls it plain 'Quercus ilex' (holm oak); the 2009 government decree gives the more exact hybrid/intergrade taxon quoted above. Recorded both; the writer should use holm oak as the common name and can mention the hybrid detail as a curiosity if it fits.

DIMENSIONS: Wikipedia gives height 11m and trunk diameter 1.30m (explicitly 'diametroan', diameter, NOT circumference). girth_cm above (410) is DERIVED by multiplying that diameter by pi (130cm x pi = ~408cm), not a source's own circumference figure; flag this conversion for the writer rather than presenting 410 as measured.

AGE: Wikipedia's own wording is vague and I kept it vague per the rule: 'one of the oldest trees in Navarre, over 500 years old' ('500 urte baino gehiago'), and that it was already a young tree ('gaztetxo') when Castile conquered Upper Navarre (the Conquest of Navarre by Castile was 1512-1524). Nobody gives a precise figure; age_min/max above is a generous band around the stated floor, not a new estimate of my own.

STORY MATERIAL: it was the FIRST tree on Navarre's original 1991 monumental-tree list (Decreto Foral 165/1991), i.e. Navarre's own Monumento Natural No. 1 among trees. Of three original main limbs, only one remains; the trunk has grown lopsided and partly hollow leaning toward that surviving limb, but Wikipedia describes it as still standing and sound ('zutik eta sendo dirau'). In 2022 the local council (Ayuntamiento de Yerri-Deierri) and its Basque-language service commissioned an illustrated audio tale for children built around this specific tree and a Basque mythological figure (Basajaun), which is decent circumstantial evidence the tree was still a going local landmark as recently as 2022 (source: kotarro.eus/event/audio-ipuina-eta-ibilaldia-eraulgo-artea, not fetched directly, so not counted as one of the two verified sources, but noted here). No death/felling report found anywhere.

ACCESS: no register vitality/access field, but nothing anywhere suggests restricted land; it stands beside an ordinary rural track, visible from the village. Treating as free and open per the OSM/register-silence convention.

DESTINATION CALL: this is a genuinely old, individually named, government-designated single oak in a village of a few dozen people, in a remote Navarre valley. It clears the single-famous-tree bar on 'genuinely remarkable and individually documented' but NOT obviously on 'would somebody travel specifically for THIS tree' the way the Angel Oak or a truly monumental specimen would: it is modest in dimensions (11m tall, ~1.3m diameter) next to Spain's true giants. It is 34.7km from Pamplona (which we already publish) and 52.7km from Vitoria-Gasteiz (unpublished) — both too far for a day-trip/30-minute-transport boundary, and there is no realistic public transport link at all, only a car. It does not cluster within 2km of Garaiko artea (71km away), Ondategiko Haritza (61.8km) or Roble Escarcio (110.7km), nor of any other of the four candidates in this batch. Recording the verified facts here; whether it ever gets a page of its own (single-famous-tree exception) or waits as a lead is not mine to decide.

name: Garaiko artea (the Encina de Garai / Encina de Etxeita)
age_estimate: documented only as "centenaria" (very old); no numeric age given by any source

location.address: In the meadow of the Etxeita farmhouse, opposite the Santa Kataliñe/Santa Catalina hermitage, off the BI-3341 road between Goiuria (Iurreta) and Garai, Garai, Bizkaia
location.neighbourhood: Etxeita caserio grounds, Garai (Durangaldea district), Bizkaia

access: Free but on working farmland: from the Santa Catalina/Santa Kataliñe hermitage on the BI-3341 between Goiuria and Garai, a paved track crosses about 800m of pine wood to the Etxeita farmhouse; the tree stands in the meadow just north of the farm buildings. The official Bizkaia government listing notes an information panel stands at the tree, and a Basque tourism site (MugaKultura, Oct 2025) gives these exact directions and actively invites visitors, while asking them to respect the place and the people who live there. Flagging for a future access check (e.g. OSM path tags) rather than treating the farmhouse setting as settled.
transport: Rural Durangaldea, Bizkaia; no public transport reaches the farm track. Garai and neighbouring Iurreta are about 26km from Bilbao (which we already publish); a car is the realistic way to reach it.
verify_notes:
THREE SOURCES, well past the two-source bar: (1) bizkaia.eus, the Diputacion Foral de Bizkaia's own official monumental-tree register page, listing this as Natural Monument 'Encina de Garai (ES213002)', species 'Quercus ilex ilex', with coordinates Lat 43.19801828 / Long -2.62562536 (matches this lead's coordinate, 43.197819/-2.625761, to within a few metres, so location_precision is confirmed on the register's own tree-level coordinate); (2) es.wikipedia.org's 'Arboles singulares de la Comunidad Autonoma del Pais Vasco' article, an independent encyclopedia entry with its own description and citations; (3) mugakultura.eus, a Basque local-culture/tourism site's article dated 2025-10-23 (fetched and read directly, not taken from a search summary), marking the tree's 30th anniversary of protection and confirming it is still standing and actively promoted as a place to visit AS OF LATE 2025, which is good recent alive-evidence.

DESIGNATION: protected since 1995 under Decreto 265/1995 (Gobierno Vasco), one of the Basque Country's first legally protected singular trees; it automatically became a legal 'monumento natural' under later Basque conservation law per the bizkaia.eus page's own text.

DIMENSIONS: the bizkaia.eus register gives an actual TRUNK figure, not a search-summary guess: 5.7m perimeter measured at 1.3m height (girth_cm 570 above is this measured figure, not derived), stem/bole height 0.8m, total height 8.5m, crown diameter 20m. Wikipedia and MugaKultura both separately describe the CROWN (not the trunk) as having a circumference of 'more than 60 metres' and a diameter of 'more than 19 metres', consistent with the register's 20m crown-diameter figure; do not let the writer confuse the ~60m CROWN circumference with the tree's actual 5.7m TRUNK girth, they describe different things.

AGE: no source anywhere gives a number. Wikipedia's generic list labels it 'Centenario' (i.e. very old, unspecified) and MugaKultura calls it 'esta encina centenaria'; both are vague and I kept them vague per the rule rather than inventing a figure. Recorded age_min/age_max as null (empty) rather than guessing from girth, because I have no published Quercus ilex growth-rate figure to derive from and the sources themselves decline to give a number; a reader with local knowledge or a dendrologist could answer this on the page.

STORY MATERIAL: shaped by generations of pruning to feed livestock on its acorns, which gave it the wide symmetrical crown; oral tradition says a flock of up to 360 sheep has sheltered under it. Views over the Durangaldea mountains from the meadow.

ACCESS, the genuinely open question: the tree stands on the grounds of a still-working, apparently inhabited farmhouse (Etxeita). This is NOT a doorbell-and-permission case (no source describes needing to ask anyone, there is a marked track and an official information panel, and a tourism site actively gives turn-by-turn directions and encourages the visit), but it is also not an unambiguous public park either, and the tourism piece explicitly asks visitors to be respectful of the people living there. I am delivering this per 'publish what verifies, the access call gets an honest caveat rather than a hold', flagging it so a later pass can settle it further with an OSM foot/access tag check on the BI-3341-to-Etxeita track (the Ypres technique), which I did not have time for in this pass.

DESTINATION CALL: an individually named, 30-year-designated holm oak with a real local story (the 360 sheep, the pastoral pruning, an information panel, an active 2025 tourism write-up), but modest in absolute size (8.5m tall) and, like Eraulgo artea, sitting alone in farmland rather than in any existing cluster: 26.1km from Bilbao (published), 71km from Eraulgo artea, 28.6km from Ondategiko Haritza (the closest of the four to it, but still outside a walkable or day-trip radius), 110.8km from Roble Escarcio. Recording the verified facts; the container decision (single-famous-tree exception, a future Durangaldea/Garai cluster, or staying a lead) is not mine to force.

name: Ondategiko Haritza (the Roble de Ondategi / Roble de Sarragoa)
age_estimate: documented only as "centenario" (very old); no numeric age given by any source

location.address: On the campa (communal meadow) of Sarragoa, at the southwest edge of Ondategi, at the end of the street to the left of the church, Zigoitia, Alava/Araba
location.neighbourhood: Ondategi, a small village of Zigoitia municipality, Alava/Araba

access: Free. Stands on an open communal meadow (campa) at the village edge, reached by the street that runs left of the church; no gate, ticket or private-land caveat found in any source. Also known locally as the Roble de Sarragoa / Sarragoako haritza / Arbol gordo de Zanagua.
transport: Rural Zigoitia, Alava; no realistic public transport. About 13km from Vitoria-Gasteiz (unpublished) and 38km from Bilbao (published); a car is the realistic way to reach it.
verify_notes:
THREE INDEPENDENT SOURCES: (1) es.wikipedia.org's 'Arboles singulares de la Comunidad Autonoma del Pais Vasco' article, giving species, height and the festival history, citing the official Basque Government declaration; (2) euskal-herria.org/node/24472 (a 2011 post by a hiking/nature site contributor named Inaxio), independently confirming species, height 20m, ~30m spread, condition 'Ona' (good), and the alternate name Sarragoako haritza, and itself citing the old Eusko Jaurlaritza biodiversity database (a dead link today, http://www1.euskadi.net/biodiversidad/fichaarbol.apl, 404 and not in the Wayback Machine, so not counted as a live source, but the citation shows the underlying government designation existed at that URL); (3) paisajesdealava.blogspot.com (fetched directly, not from a search summary), which cites 'Gobierno Vasco - Eusko Jaurlaritza - Declaracion de arboles Singulares' explicitly as its source and gives the same measurements as the WebSearch AI summary, CONFIRMING those figures actually appear on a real page rather than being a search-tool invention: perimeter at 1.3m = 4.9m, bole height 2m, total height 20m, crown diameter 30m. Species, dimensions and the pre-Civil-War San Lorenzo romeria story are consistent across all three.

DESIGNATION: Singular Tree of the Basque Country since 1997, one of Alava's ten protected singular trees per the same sources; separately noted (WebSearch summary only, not independently fetched, so treated as a lead not a fact) that it featured on an ONCE lottery ticket in the 'Abraza tu arbol' series.

GIRTH: girth_cm above (490) is the register's own measured trunk PERIMETER at 1.3m, not a derived figure.

AGE: no source gives a number, only 'centenario' (an old tree, unspecified), kept vague per the rule. age_min/max left null rather than derived: I have no cited Quercus robur growth-rate figure to derive from, and inventing one from the 490cm girth alone would be exactly the kind of guess this project forbids.

LOCATION: I could not find an official government coordinate fetched directly (unlike the Navarra and Bizkaia trees in this same batch, where the register itself gave a lat/lon); a Geocaching cache page for this tree exists (GC4EC9X) but hides its exact coordinate behind a login wall, so I could not use it. This lead's own coordinate (42.95363042, -2.73524306) is consistent with Ondategi village's known location, and the sources agree the tree stands at the SOUTHWEST EDGE of the village on the Sarragoa meadow, next to the street left of the church, which is village-level/street-level knowledge rather than a surveyed tree point. Marking location_precision 'approximate' honestly rather than upgrading it on no real evidence.

STORY MATERIAL: for generations gave shade and shelter to livestock and people at village festivals; until the Spanish Civil War the village held its San Lorenzo romeria (10 August) under its crown, with a lone accordion player providing music because the village could only afford paid musicians for the Santa Lucia festival (13 December). A good, specific, sourced anecdote.

ACCESS: a communal village meadow at a street's end, no restriction found anywhere; this is the most straightforwardly open-access tree of the four in this batch.

DESTINATION CALL: individually named, government-designated since 1997, with a genuine, specific historical anecdote (the pre-war romeria) that the other three trees in this batch lack. Still modest in scale next to Spain's true giants, and geographically isolated from any published place: 13.0km from Vitoria-Gasteiz (unpublished, and even that is beyond an easy walk), 38km from Bilbao (published), 28.6km from Garaiko artea (the nearest of this batch), 61.8km from Eraulgo artea, 83.1km from Roble Escarcio. Recording the verified facts; the container decision is not mine to force, though of the four in this batch this is the one I would flag as having the strongest standalone story.

name: Roble Escarcio

location.address: Alone in an open meadow on the ridge facing the village, about 500m along a farm track west of Villamudria, Rabanos municipality, province of Burgos, Castilla y Leon
location.neighbourhood: Villamudria, a hamlet of the municipality of Rabanos, Burgos

access: Free and public (one source explicitly rates access as 'Publica' and difficulty 'Facil'): from the village, walk past the first row of houses and take the track continuing the road's direction; after about 500m the tree stands alone on an open, treeless plain, and the correct fork at the only junction leads straight to it.
transport: Rural Burgos province; no public transport reaches Villamudria. About 33km from Burgos city (which we do not currently publish); a car is the realistic way to reach it.
verify_notes:
CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: this tree is NOT in the Basque Country. Villamudria/Rabanos is in the province of Burgos, Castilla y Leon, on the north slope of the Sierra de la Demanda, roughly 110km south of the other three Basque candidates in this batch. Flagging this plainly rather than silently filing it as Basque; it came from the same _famous-spain.json leads file but is a different region entirely.

TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES, both fetched directly (not from a search summary): (1) arbolessingularescyl.blogspot.com, a specialist blog run by Cesar Herranz Beltran, who also published a print book 'Arboles Singulares de Castilla y Leon' (sold with El Mundo newspaper per the second source); this blog entry gives species, height, form and age; (2) tierrasdeburgos.blogspot.com, an independent hiking/local-heritage blog by a different author ('Montacedo'), describing an actual visit on foot, turn-by-turn directions from the village, and explicitly citing 'el listado de arboles protegidos por la Junta de Castilla y Leon' (the regional government's own protected-tree list) as the tree's designation basis. A third search (not fetched directly, so not counted as a source, but corroborating context) confirms the Junta de Castilla y Leon runs an official 'Catalogo de Especies Vegetales Singulares' under Ley 8/1991, with 143 trees formally catalogued by a 2003 decree, and open GIS layers (IDECyL, datosabiertos.jcyl.es 'Mapa de Arboles Singulares de Castilla y Leon') that I did not have time to query directly in this pass; a future pass could pull the exact official coordinate and catalogue number from there.

SPECIES: Quercus pyrenaica (Pyrenean oak, aka melojo/rebollo), consistent across both sources; monumentaltrees.com's Spanish listing (found by search, titled 'Rebollo Roble Escarcio', rebollo being a common name for this same species) independently agrees but its page 403s automated fetches per the known blocklist pattern, so it was NOT fetched and is used only as the cross-check hard rule 1 allows, not as one of the two required sources.

GIRTH: tierrasdeburgos gives 'la 7 metros de perimetro nominal' (7m 'nominal' perimeter, their own hedge-word); the other blog's post (fetched but its table formatting broke under extraction) showed numbers consistent with a girth in the 6.8-7.75m range alongside a 16.5m height figure; an earlier web search (not independently re-verified on the page itself) had cited 7.25m measured 2016-11-04. I recorded girth_cm as 700 (the plainest, most directly quoted figure) and flagged the 7.0-7.75m spread for the writer rather than picking a falsely precise number.

AGE: both sources independently say 'unos 600 anos' / 'edad estimada de 600 anos' (about 600 years), which I kept as the vague figure the sources themselves give rather than sharpening it; age_min/max above is a band around that stated figure, not a new derivation of my own. Cesar Javier Palacios's book 'Arboles Singulares de Burgos' (mentioned by the tierrasdeburgos post as a named source that STILL could not explain the tree's isolation) apparently could not pin down more than this either.

LOCATION: this lead's coordinate (42.330542, -3.295127) sits within a few hundred metres of TWO independently geotagged Wikimedia Commons photographs of this same tree: File:Roble_Escarcio_front.jpg at 42.329795/-3.292273 and File:Roble_Escenario.jpg at 42.33109/-3.295012. I checked the brief's flagged filename concern directly: 'Roble_Escenario.jpg' (escenario = stage/scenery, not escarcio) is filed under Commons Category:Roble_Escarcio and its coordinate matches the other file's within ~250m, so this reads as a genuine upload typo rather than a different tree; both photos are of this same oak. The tree is also explicitly described by an eyewitness (tierrasdeburgos) as standing ALONE in an open, currently treeless plain with no other trees nearby to confuse it with, which is exactly the case the aerial/photo-position evidence rule allows for confirming a position from a mapped, identifiable single crown. On that basis I am marking location_precision 'confirmed' rather than 'approximate', though the ~250-300m spread between the two Commons geotags and this lead's own point means the pin should sit somewhere in that small cluster rather than trusting any one coordinate to the metre.

STORY MATERIAL: stands alone and unpruned in what was likely farmed or grazed land until fairly recently, which is itself the local mystery: nobody, including a published local-trees book, has explained why this one oak was left standing while its surroundings were cleared. Its hollow trunk has an opening you can see into. Locals used its shade in summer and gathered its large acorns; shepherds reportedly used the hollow trunk as a shelter and even lit fires in it ('utilizado por los pastores para refugio y chimenea'), which the visiting blogger calls 'not very encouraging' for the tree's future condition, a small honest caveat worth keeping rather than smoothing over.

DESTINATION CALL: this is the most convincingly 'worth a special trip' of the four candidates in this batch on raw size and story (a genuinely isolated, ~600-year-old, 7m-girth veteran with a real unsolved local mystery attached, officially catalogued by a regional government), but it stands entirely alone: 110.7km from Eraulgo artea, 110.8km from Garaiko artea, 83.1km from Ondategiko Haritza, and 33km from Burgos (which we do not currently publish and which would need its own case made separately). It does not join any Basque cluster because it is not in the Basque Country at all; if this ever gets a page it would most naturally be as its own single-famous-tree entry, or eventually paired with a future Burgos-area page, not with the other three trees in this batch. Recording the verified facts; the container decision is not mine to force.

name: Pino del Aprisquillo
species: Spanish Black Pine (Pinus nigra subsp. salzmannii)

location.address: Beside the Arroyo del Aprisquillo in the Garganta/Charco de la Hoya gorge, below the Cerro de la Escusa, La Adrada, Avila province, Castilla y Leon
location.neighbourhood: Charco de la Hoya gorge, eastern foothills of the Sierra de Gredos, La Adrada

access: Free, on public forest tracks. Two marked hiking routes reach it (from the road to the Colmenilla dam, or via Canto de la Linde), both with real elevation gain (roughly 630m over a 10km round trip per rutinasvarias); one alternative interior trail is described as not fully signposted. The municipality installed new trail signage for this specific route in November 2023, and a 2024 hiker reported the final stretch overgrown, so the walk is real but rougher than a park path.
transport: Rural Avila province; no public transport reaches the trailhead. La Adrada is about 85km southwest of Madrid (published) and roughly 45km from Avila city; a car to the village, then the hike, is the only realistic route.
verify_notes:
FOUR SOURCES fetched directly (none from search summaries alone), all describing the same specific named specimen: (1) arbolesdeltietar.blogspot.com (2010), a specialist local-trees blog giving species, ~5m perimeter, ~400 years, and the two access routes; (2) avilared.com (a regional news outlet), reporting the tree won Spain's 'Arbol del Ano' (Tree of the Year) 2016 vote and was selected as Spain's candidate for European Tree of the Year 2017, calling it 'pino cascalbo' locally, giving height and 'over 400 years'; (3) rutinasvarias.com, a hiking-route blog with its own visit, giving height 26m, perimeter 5.6m, diameter 1.5m, age 350 years, and noting it stands 'erguido bajo el Cerro de la Escusa'; (4) laadrada.net, the village's own tourism pages, giving base circumference 5.90m, height ~25m, calling it 'cascalvo' (same colloquial name, whitish-bark black pine). A fifth, cesefor.com (a forestry-sector news site), independently confirms the European Tree of the Year 2017 finalist status without giving dimensions.

SPECIES: confirmed to subspecies level directly from a Wikimedia Commons file's own metadata (not a source I am counting as one of the two, but strong corroboration): the geotagged photograph 'File:2017 Aprisquillo Pine ES.jpg', credited to 'P. Nogueras, Excelentisima Diputacion de Avila' (the provincial government) and sourced to treeoftheyear.org, carries a German caption identifying it explicitly as 'Schwarzkiefer "Aprisquillo" (Pinus nigra subsp. salzmannii)'. That matches monumentaltrees.com's Spanish listing title 'Pino salgareño Pino Aprisquillo' found by search (monumentaltrees.com itself 403s automated fetches, so used only as the cross-check hard rule 1 allows, not as a source). 'Laricio', 'salgareno' and 'cascalbo/cascalvo' are all colloquial Spanish names locals and blogs use interchangeably for this same taxon (Pinus nigra subsp. salzmannii, Spanish black pine), not different trees or a taxonomic disagreement.

DIMENSIONS: girth ranges 500-590cm across sources (arbolesdeltietar ~5m 'a la altura de medida reglamentaria', rutinasvarias 5.6m, laadrada.net 5.90m base circumference); recorded girth_cm as 550, a midpoint, flagging the spread rather than presenting one figure as exact. Height similarly ranges 25-43m across sources (avilared's 43m looks like an outlier against the other three clustered at 25-30m; I did not use 43m for that reason, though it appears repeated in some later aggregator listicles). Diameter 1.5m (rutinasvarias) is roughly consistent with a girth in the 470-590cm band via circumference = diameter x pi (471cm), which is a reasonable cross-check rather than a contradiction.

AGE: 'approximately 400 years' (arbolesdeltietar), 'over 400 years' (avilared), '350 years' (rutinasvarias). Kept as a band (350-450) around the vaguely and consistently stated figure rather than sharpening to one number; no source gives a documented planting date, so this is the sources' own vague estimate repeated, not a derivation of my own.

ALIVE: the tree is not a static relic. laadrada.net (municipal tourism pages, presumably current), and search results describing November 2023 trail signage installed specifically for the 'Ruta del Pino Aprisquillo', a November 2024 hiker's trip report describing the trail conditions, and the tree's inclusion in the route of the 'La Adrada Trail 2026' mountain race (25km) are all recent, independent evidence the tree and its access route are actively maintained and visited as of 2023-2026. No death or felling report found anywhere; avilared notes it 'ha sobrevivido a plagas, incendios y avatares' (has survived plagues, fires and hardships), consistent with continued good health being part of its own public story.

LOCATION: latitude/longitude above are read directly from the geotag embedded in the Commons photograph described above (40.354280, -4.635910), which is a photograph credited to the Avila provincial government and submitted for the Tree of the Year contest, i.e. a mapped photo of this specific tree rather than a village-level guess. This differs by about 3.4km from the Castilla y Leon tourism portal's own map-link coordinate for the ROUTE (40.324437, -4.649069), which is a trailhead/start-of-route pin, not the tree; I used the tree's own geotag rather than the trailhead pin. Marking location_precision 'confirmed' on the strength of that mapped, credited photograph, consistent with the aerial/photo-position evidence rule ('a mapped photo' counts as tree-level).

DESTINATION CALL: this clears 'worth the trip on its own' cleanly. It is a national title holder (Spain's Tree of the Year 2016) and an international finalist (European Tree of the Year 2017, one of sixteen national candidates), which is a real, checkable superlative rather than a vague 'protected' designation, plus a genuine hike through a gorge to reach it. It stands alone: 85km from Madrid (published) and far outside any day-trip/30-minute-transport boundary, reachable only by car, so it does not join any existing container. Recording the verified facts here per 'publish what verifies, the container decision (single-famous-tree exception vs staying a well-documented lead) is not mine to force', though of the batch this is the strongest single-tree case: a real, external, competitive title plus a specific hike people already organise trail races and signposted routes around.

name: Olmo de Navajas

location.address: Plaza del Olmo, next to the town hall, Navajas, Castellon province, Comunitat Valenciana
location.neighbourhood: Plaza del Olmo (Elm Square), village centre, Navajas

access: Free. Stands on a raised circular stone platform in the town's main square, right beside the ayuntamiento (town hall); Camino del Cid's own visitor page says the plaza is reachable directly by car and open to all, no restriction of any kind, and it hosts the village's markets, festivals and bullfighting events, so it is in continuous public use rather than roped off.
transport: Navajas has its own station on the Cercanias Valencia line C-5 (Zaragoza-Sagunto railway), but the line runs a slow, sparse regional service (about three trains a day) and the town is well beyond a 30-minute ride from Valencia; as of the time of this pass the Sagunto-Caudiel stretch is reported suspended for engineering works with a replacement bus. About 47km north of Valencia (published) by road; treated as its own place rather than a Valencia day trip.
verify_notes:
THREE SOURCES fetched directly: (1) valenciabonita.es (a Valencia-region lifestyle/news site), giving species Ulmus minor Mill., height 13.87m, perimeter 6.30m, canopy spread ~227 sq m, the 1636 planting date and planter's name (Roque Pastor), the circular platform (~7m diameter, 1.4m high) it stands on, its place on the town's coat of arms (Decreto 562/1961), and its Comunitat Valenciana monumental-tree catalogue listing; (2) xn--arbolybosquedelao-uxb.es (a Spanish tree-of-the-year archive site), independently giving the same species, planting date and planter, height 19m, age 382 (as counted in 2018/19), the same 1961 coat-of-arms decree, a 2002 Spanish postage-cancellation feature, a 2011 ONCE lottery-ticket feature, and explicitly that the tree 'has not been affected by Dutch elm disease' (grafiosis), despite that pandemic having killed most of Europe's mature elms; (3) caminodelcid.org (a regional tourist-route site), again independently giving species, height 19m, girth 6.5m, the 1636/Morisco-expulsion planting story, plaza-side location next to the ayuntamiento, and open, no-restriction, year-round access by car.

All three independently and consistently confirm this is Spain's 'Arbol del Ano' (Tree of the Year) 2019, chosen by national public vote, and Spain's entry in the European Tree of the Year 2019 contest (a WebSearch summary said it placed 12th there; not independently fetched from the contest's own site, so treated as likely but unconfirmed detail, kept out of the record).

SPECIES: Ulmus minor Mill. (field elm / common elm), consistent across all three sources and matching Wikidata's own entry (Q105762033, 'Elm from Navajas'), which separately confirms this is a distinct, individually notable specimen rather than a generic village tree.

DIMENSIONS: height given as 13.87m (valenciabonita) versus 19m (the other two); girth given as 6.30m versus 6.5m, which agree closely. I did not find a way to resolve the height discrepancy from the sources themselves (one may be measuring to the crown's visible top versus a different reference point, or one figure may be an error propagated between the aggregator sites); recorded girth_cm as 640 (midpoint of 630-650) and flagged the height spread for the writer rather than picking one figure as authoritative.

AGE: 1636 is a documented planting date FOR THIS SPECIMEN (not a bridge claim from the plaza's or village's history: the story is specifically that this elm was planted after the 1609 expulsion of the Moriscos as a symbol of the new settlers' unity, and its own name plaza and coat of arms confirm it is the same individual tree that story is about), so age_min/max (385/395) is a real, tightly-bounded estimate rather than a vague repetition.

ALIVE: xn--arbolybosquedelao explicitly states the tree remains unaffected by Dutch elm disease, which is meaningful given that pandemic has killed the great majority of Europe's large elms; a further WebSearch turned up nothing suggesting death, felling or serious decline, and its continued central role in village festivals (per caminodelcid) is itself evidence of current, maintained presence. No precise dated 2020s photo was fetched in this pass, so recorded as flagged rather than fully closed on recency, but three consistent independent descriptions with no contrary signal is a reasonable bar.

LOCATION: latitude/longitude match, to five decimal places, both a geotagged Commons photograph (File:2019 Elm of Navajas ES.jpg, credited to J.M. Ferrando via treeoftheyear.org) and Wikidata's own coordinate claim on its dedicated 'Elm from Navajas' item (Q105762033, precision ~2.8e-6 degrees, i.e. metre-scale). Two independently sourced tree-level points agreeing to five decimals, for a tree whose exact plaza and platform are independently described by three sources, is as solid as this project's location bar gets; marked confirmed.

DESTINATION CALL: clears 'worth the trip on its own' well. A national Tree of the Year title (2019), a specific and checkable founding story (planted 1636 as a post-expulsion unity symbol, still named on the coat of arms and the town hymn), a genuinely single collectible point (one tree, on its own named plaza, no ambiguity about which tree or where to stand), full free access, and the added, checkable rarity of a mature elm untouched by Dutch elm disease. It sits about 47km from Valencia (published) with no fast public transport link, well outside a 30-minute day-trip boundary, so it does not join Valencia's page; it stands on its own single-famous-tree merits instead. Recording the verified facts; the container decision (single-famous-tree exception vs staying a lead) is not mine to force, though this is the strongest-documented candidate in the batch after the Aprisquillo pine, arguably ahead of it on the strength of the exact, corroborated pin and the founding-story specificity.

name: Pino-Roble de Canicosa de la Sierra
species: Pyrenean Oak (Quercus pyrenaica) with a Scots Pine (Pinus sylvestris) growing out of its hollow trunk
age_estimate: oak about 250 years, pine growing from within it about 130 years

location.address: Paraje El Piquillo, beside the road (BU-V-8227) from Canicosa de la Sierra towards Navaleno, about 2km from the village then 1km on a marked path, Canicosa de la Sierra, Burgos province, Castilla y Leon
location.neighbourhood: El Piquillo, an aged rebollo (Pyrenean oak) dehesa at about 1,200m altitude, Canicosa de la Sierra

access: Free, on communal land beside a public road. lagunasdeneila.es gives turn-by-turn directions: take the BU-V-8227 towards Navaleno, about 2km out of the village there is a painted roadside rock marked 'Pino Roble' and a small dirt parking area, then roughly 1km on a marked path to the tree. canicosa.info independently confirms it stands right beside that same road with views back to the village. One source (tierrasdeburgos) calls it 'not especially signposted' and easy to walk past even with coordinates, which is a real caveat about how inconspicuous the pair looks against the surrounding forest, not an access restriction.
transport: Rural Sierra de la Demanda, Burgos province; no public transport. About 60km from Burgos city and roughly 50km from Soria (neither currently published); realistically reached by car to the village and then the short walk described above.
verify_notes:
This is not a single tree but a genuine, well-documented natural curiosity: an old Pyrenean oak (Quercus pyrenaica, locally 'rebollo' or 'melojo') with a Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris, 'pino albar') that germinated inside a hollow in its trunk, most likely from a pinecone a squirrel carried in, and has grown up through and out of the host oak, splitting its bark and accelerating its decay as it grows. Treating this as ONE collectible point (the ensemble itself, at one obvious place to stand, per the Lomanstraat precedent for a compact famous pairing) rather than two separate trees.

FOUR SOURCES fetched directly, all consistent: (1) canicosa.info/PinoRoble, an apparently dedicated project/heritage site for the tree, giving the most precise figures found anywhere: pine height 15m, oak height 12.5m, oak circumference 3.40m, pine circumference 2.00m measured at 2.9m height, oak diameter ~2m, altitude 1,200m, communal ownership, and explicitly 'sin medidas de conservacion' (no conservation measures currently in place) and 'sintomas de decadencia' (signs of decline) in the oak; (2) tierrasdeburgos.blogspot.com, an independent visited-it-myself hiking blog, giving the same ~250/~130 year ages, a coordinate (41.93069, -3.04157) that sits within about 100m of this lead's own coordinate, i.e. two independent sources placing the same tree-level point; (3) lagunasdeneila.es, a regional visitor-information site, giving the same ages, the 2016 European Tree of the Year fifth-place result (out of trees representing 15 countries), and the turn-by-turn directions in the access field above; (4) cesefor.com, a forestry-sector news outlet, confirming the tree was chosen in late 2015 as Spain's representative for the European Tree of the Year 2016 contest and describing the same formation story. A WebSearch-only figure (Quercus pyrenaica as the exact species rather than plain 'roble') was cross-checked and repeated across enough independent hits, including asturnatura.com's species page and a Revista Quercus Facebook post, that I am treating it as established rather than a search-summary invention, though no single fetched primary source spelled out the Latin binomial itself.

AGES: both figures (~250 years oak, ~130 years pine) are repeated identically and vaguely across all four sources with no numeric derivation shown; kept as the sources' own vague estimate (banded 220-280 for the oak, the older and defining component) rather than sharpened. girth_cm above (340) is the oak's own measured circumference from canicosa.info, not derived; the pine's separate circumference (200cm at 2.9m height, an unusually high measurement point because that is where the pine's own trunk clears the oak's crown) is recorded here rather than in the girth field because the schema holds one figure and the oak is the older, defining host.

ALIVE: no source reports collapse, felling or death. canicosa.info's 'signs of decline' is a real, honest caveat: the pine's growth is actively tearing the oak's trunk and there are no conservation measures in place, so this is a curiosity in active, ongoing decay rather than a stable specimen, and a future pass or reader should recheck it periodically. A Spanish car forum (forocoches.com, thread dated 22 August 2025) discussing this specific tree by name is recent, if informal, evidence people were still visiting and talking about it as of last month.

LOCATION: this lead's coordinate (41.93133, -3.04235) sits within roughly 100m of an independent hiking blogger's own GPS reading of the same tree (41.93069, -3.04157), which I am treating as two independent tree-level fixes agreeing closely, rather than a village-level guess; a Google-Maps-derived coordinate found via a third site (pinaresyelvalle.com, 41.9672, -3.0684) sits about 4.5km away and looks like an imprecise reference to the general area rather than the tree, so I did not use it. Marking location_precision 'confirmed' on the two closer, mutually corroborating fixes.

DESTINATION CALL: this is a real natural curiosity, not merely an old tree: two different species fused into one visible, photographable formation, a genuine talking point (it even inspired the name and form of a modern building, the 'Pino-Roble House' by architect Valentin Arrieta Berdasco, per ArchDaily), and a real external superlative (fifth place, European Tree of the Year 2016, representing Spain). It clears 'would somebody travel specifically for this' on rarity and story rather than on size. It stands alone: no published city sits within any reasonable cluster distance (Burgos city ~60km, Soria ~50km, neither published; the batch's own esc_001 Roble Escarcio, also in Burgos province, is about 48km away, too far to cluster), and no public transport reaches it. Recording the verified facts; the container decision (single-famous-tree exception vs staying a lead) is not mine to force, though the genuine oddity here (a living symbiosis actively destroying its host, an architecture reference, a European contest placing) makes a reasonable case for its own page.

name: Olmo centenario de Millena (Om centenari de Millena)

location.address: Plaza de la Iglesia de Sant Josep, Millena, El Comtat, Alicante province, Comunitat Valenciana
location.neighbourhood: Church square (Plaza de la Iglesia), village centre of Millena

access: Free. Stands in the open church square (Plaza de la Iglesia de Sant Josep) in the centre of the small village of Millena (population around 200); lacantimploraverde.es describes it as easy to find, with the village itself putting up signage pointing visitors to it at the entrance to town.
transport: Rural inland Alicante province (El Comtat comarca), between Gorga and Cocentaina; no public transport reaches the village. Roughly 65km from Alicante city (published) and well outside any day-trip boundary from it; realistically reached by car, e.g. from Cocentaina or Alcoi (neither currently published).
verify_notes:
THREE SOURCES fetched directly (none from search-summary figures alone): (1) lacantimploraverde.es (2015), a travel blog with its own visit and photos, giving the plaza location, the local legend that it is popularly called 'Olmo milenario' (thousand-year elm) though the blogger's own theory ties planting to the 1812 Cadiz Constitution ('La Pepa', elms were symbolically planted across Spanish towns then) for an age of ~203 years -- this specific '1812 planting' theory is the AUTHOR'S OWN SPECULATION, not a documented planting record for this specimen, so I am not treating it as a derived age (it is exactly the kind of bridge claim BRIEF_RESEARCH.md warns about: a general planting custom joined to one unconfirmed tree). The same source states explicitly the tree is NOT on the official Catalogo de arboles monumentales y singulares de la Comunitat Valenciana, but is generically protected under Ley 4/2006 de Patrimonio Arboreo Monumental de la Comunidad Valenciana, and calls it 'the last plaza elm in good health in Alicante province', with support pillars added after a snow-laden branch broke. (2) practicomagazine.com (2016), an independent regional-tourism magazine piece on Millena, giving diameter 5m and height 10m and calling it 'tricentenario' (three-hundred-year-old), confirming the plaza location. (3) geocaching.com's own cache page for 'Om mil.lenari / Olmo milenario' at this site, giving height 10m, trunk circumference 5.30m, crown diameter up to 11m, repeating the 300+ years estimate, the same 'last healthy plaza elm in the province' claim, the same Ley 4/2006 protection and the same Dutch-elm-disease (grafiosis) context. Three independent sources agree closely on the dimensions (girth ~530cm) and on the vague '300 years' figure, so age_estimate is kept as the sources' own vague repeated figure ('roughly 300 years', banded 200-300) rather than sharpened, and the 1812-planting theory is left out of age_min/max entirely, recorded here only as colour for the writer.

GIRTH: recorded girth_cm as 530 (the geocache page's 5.30m trunk circumference), corroborated by practicomagazine's 5m diameter figure (5m diameter implies ~1571cm circumference via pi, which does NOT match 530cm circumference -- practicomagazine's 'diametro' figure looks like a loose/incorrect use of the word, most likely meaning crown spread or a misstatement, since 530cm circumference implies a trunk diameter of only ~169cm; flagging this unit/word confusion rather than silently picking one).

SPECIES: Ulmus minor (field elm/common elm), consistent across all three sources and with the Commons category name ('om' is Catalan/Valencian for elm); no source gives finer taxonomic detail, in line with the usual local-name-only situation.

ALIVE: all three sources describe an actively maintained, currently standing tree (support pillars added and later one pillar itself damaged by a subsequent snowfall, per the geocache page), and three Commons photographs by a known Catalan tree photographer (Joanbanjo) are dated 2013-06-02, showing roots, bark and branches in apparently healthy condition. No death, felling or decline report found in any search. However nothing found is dated later than 2016, so recency is thinner than ideal; flagging on that basis per the bar (confirmation thin rather than absent) rather than holding the tree back.

LOCATION: the lead's coordinate (38.730569, -0.363691) is NOT a tree-level fix -- none of the three 2013 Commons photos of this tree carry a geotag (checked directly via the Commons API), and this exact coordinate matches to five decimal places the OSM administrative-boundary CENTROID for the village of Millena as a whole (Nominatim: 38.7305669, -0.3638185), i.e. it is a village-level point that happens to sit close to the plaza because Millena is a very small, compact village (~215 residents). An Overpass query for the village's own church (Esglesia de Sant Josep de Millena, way 753200043) returns 38.7307031, -0.3635072, about 22m from the lead coordinate and consistent with all sources placing the tree in that church's own square. Marking location_precision 'approximate': we know the plaza with confidence (in front of the Church of Sant Josep, centre of Millena) but not a tree-level pin, and the given coordinate should be read as 'the village/plaza area', not 'the trunk'.

DESTINATION CALL: a real, checkable curiosity (explicitly the last healthy plaza elm surviving Dutch elm disease in the whole of Alicante province, per two independent sources) with genuine size for the species (530cm girth, comparable to Navajas's verified 630-650cm elm) and a visible, photographable detail (the support pillars holding up its heavy limbs). It has no national Tree-of-the-Year title or Wikidata item of its own (checked, none found), so it is a notch below Navajas's or Aprisquillo's documentation. It sits about 65km from Alicante (published) with no transit link, well outside any day-trip boundary, and there is no other published or nearby-verified tree to cluster it with, so it stands alone or waits as a well-documented lead; recording the verified facts either way per 'publish what verifies, the container decision is not mine to force'.
